hero.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect June 30 in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties to protect waterways
hero.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will ban any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen starting June 30. Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County said the ban is to help reduce nutrient rich run off during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms.

Those blooms could disrupt waterways like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. Skaggs said algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health.

Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, said a good alternative during the ban is using composting for gardens and landscaping. Ricketts said composting can be done in a small trash can, which is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape.

The fertilizer ban runs through the rainy season to prevent nutrient runoff from reaching local rivers and lagoons during the period when Florida typically receives the most rainfall.

cards.headline: Fatal crash on Donald Ross Road in Jupiter kills driver Sunday morning
cards.teaser: A single-vehicle crash on Donald Ross Road in Jupiter Sunday morning killed one person, according to Jupiter police officials.
cards.body:
A single-vehicle crash on Donald Ross Road in Jupiter Sunday morning killed one person, according to Jupiter police officials. The crash happened just before 6 a.m. when the driver came over railroad tracks, lost control of the vehicle, and struck a tree, according to preliminary information from the scene. Police confirmed one adult male died in the crash but are withholding the victim's name pending notification of next of kin.

Both eastbound and westbound lanes of Donald Ross Road between Military Trail and Alternate A1A were closed for several hours as crash investigators worked the scene. The roadway has since reopened to traffic. The Jupiter Police Department is continuing to investigate the circumstances that led to the fatal crash.

cards.headline: Stuart business owner says city permit delays cost nearly $40,000, nearly two years for storage building
cards.body:
Janet Milici, co-owner of Natural Flow Impact Windows and Doors in Stuart, has spent nearly two years and almost $40,000 trying to obtain a permit for a simple storage building at her business property. She first applied in 2024 to build a 30-by-40-foot structure in the back of her property to store materials used by her company, not as part of any business expansion.

Throughout the application process, Milici says she has been required to complete multiple studies and reviews including engineering assessments, environmental evaluations, traffic analyses, and even pay for turtle relocation. "People try to cut corners and do things without permitting, but we are trying to do everything right," Milici said. Despite understanding that permitting requirements exist for good reasons, she believes the process has become unreasonably complicated for a straightforward storage project. The permit has recently been approved, but the city continues to charge additional fees as the project moves forward.

The delays have created serious problems for Milici as hurricane season began. With materials still stored outdoors while waiting for the project to be completed, she faces potential damage and significant financial losses. "The thing that bothers me is that hurricane season is here, and if I can't put my materials in a safe place, then it's going to cost me—it's going to put me out of business if you really want to know," she said. She stressed that she is simply trying to improve her property and the service she provides to customers, but feels blocked at every stage.

Milici brought her concerns to public attention after attending a Let's Hear It community meeting in Jensen Beach, deciding the issue deserved broader attention among area residents. "It's been a process, and I thought that this should be brought to everyone's attention who lives in this area," she said. WPTV has requested information from the City of Stuart's Planning and Zoning department about the standard process for obtaining storage building permits within city limits but has not yet received a response.

cards.headline: Florida Home Builders Association endorses Ashley Moody for U.S. Senate
cards.body:
The Florida Home Builders Association announced its endorsement of U.S. Senator Ashley Moody on Monday as she runs in the November general election. Moody, a Plant City Republican, was appointed to the Senate by Governor Ron DeSantis to fill the seat left vacant when Marco Rubio was confirmed as Secretary of State. This year's election will determine who serves the final two years of the six-year Senate term.

In response to the endorsement, Moody expressed her appreciation for the organization's support. "I am honored to earn the endorsement of the Florida Home Builders Association – an organization that represents the men and women who quite literally build the American Dream for Florida families," she said. Moody highlighted her work on housing issues, stating she has championed housing reform and fought to lower costs for Florida families. The construction industry has backed Moody before, endorsing her during her 2018 and 2022 campaigns for Florida Attorney General, races in which she received more votes than any candidate on the Florida ballot.

Moody has already raised substantial campaign funds for her Senate bid. Through March of this year, she had accumulated 8.2 million dollars. In the Republican primary, she faces three other candidates, though her closest competitor had raised less than 3,400 dollars by the end of March. The GOP primary will take place in August to determine the party's nominee.

On the Democratic side, Alex Vindman is positioned as the likely nominee after raising approximately 8.2 million dollars through the first quarter. However, Vindman must first compete in the Democratic primary against Angie Nixon, who had reported 294,000 dollars in fundraising through the same period. The August primary elections will decide which candidates from each party advance to the November general election, where voters will select Florida's representative for the remainder of the Senate term. Moody is seeking her first full six-year Senate term following her two successful statewide campaigns for Attorney General.

cards.headline: Stuart business owner says city permit delays cost her $40,000 over two years
cards.body:
A Stuart business owner is speaking out about what she describes as an unnecessarily complicated permit approval process for a storage building project. Janet Milici, who co-owns Natural Flow Impact Windows and Doors, decided to share her experience after attending a community meeting in Jensen Beach. She filed her initial application in 2024 to construct a 30-by-40-foot storage building at the back of her business property. The structure was designed to store materials used in her day-to-day operations, not to expand the business itself.

Throughout the permitting process, Milici faced multiple requirements that she believes went beyond what was necessary for a simple storage building. The city required her to complete engineering studies, environmental reviews, and traffic analyses. She was also required to pay for turtle relocation. All of these additional steps added up financially, with Milici estimating she has spent approximately $40,000 to navigate the approval process. While she understands that permitting requirements exist for good reasons, Milici believes the demands placed on her project have been excessive. "All I am trying to do is improve my property. I am trying to improve the service we can give our customers, and it's like the city is shooting us down at every turn," she said.

The timing of the delays has created a significant problem for her business operations. With hurricane season now underway, materials that should be stored safely inside the building remain exposed outdoors. This vulnerability concerns Milici, who worries about potential damage and the financial impact on her company. "The thing that bothers me is that hurricane season is here, and if I can't put my materials in a safe place, then it's going to cost me—it's going to put me out of business if you really want to know," she said. Despite her frustrations with the process, Milici emphasized that she chose to pursue proper permitting rather than cut corners. "People try to cut corners and do things without permitting, but we are trying to do everything right," she noted.

The permit has recently received approval, but Milici still faces additional city fees as the project enters its final stages. She felt her situation was important enough to bring to public attention, hoping others in the area would become aware of the challenges involved in the local permitting process. WPTV reached out to the City of Stuart's Planning and Zoning department for comment on the permit procedures for storage buildings within city limits but has not yet received a response.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested for allegedly chasing children with baseball bat
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man faces arrest after allegedly chasing children with a baseball bat.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested a man accused of chasing children while armed with a baseball bat. The incident prompted law enforcement response and led to the man's arrest.

Details about the circumstances of the incident, the number of children involved, and specific charges filed against the suspect were not provided in available records. The arrest took place in Port St. Lucie.

cards.headline: Indian River County voters face decision on renewing $40 lagoon tax
cards.body:
Indian River County residents will decide whether to renew a $40 annual tax dedicated to Indian River Lagoon restoration efforts. The tax generates funding for lagoon cleanup and environmental restoration projects that have been underway in the county.

The renewal vote will determine whether gains made in lagoon restoration continue or face potential setbacks. The tax assessment has funded local environmental initiatives aimed at improving water quality and habitat restoration in the Indian River Lagoon system.

The Indian River Lagoon spans multiple counties along Florida's east coast and has faced ongoing environmental challenges requiring sustained restoration funding. Indian River County's portion of the restoration work depends on the continuation of the local tax revenue stream.

Voters will make their decision on the $40 annual assessment renewal in an upcoming ballot measure. The tax has been a dedicated revenue source for lagoon restoration work in Indian River County since its initial approval.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old Orion Jean Baptiste launches junior chess club at Morningside Library
cards.teaser: A new juniors chess club has launched in Port St. Lucie, inspired by a 9-year-old boy who wanted to share his love of the game with his community.
cards.body:
Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, launched a new juniors chess club inspired by his passion for the game, which began at age 5 playing with family. "I just wanted kids to learn about chess," Baptiste said. He hopes to shift focus away from technology toward board games, saying "Everybody's more focused on like tech stuff. I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games." The Atlantis Chess Club now meets at the Port St. Lucie Morningside Library every Friday, with more than 36 juniors already joined. The club will soon begin two additional programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce.

Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, believes chess will develop stronger leaders. "[It] will help to build leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision [making]," Kempton said. The club attracts players of all skill levels. Thomas Furlong brought his children to participate, noting "This is like the perfect chance for her to learn chess, my son to get better at chess and then them to have a little sibling rivalry competition." His daughter Francesca, one of the club's newest members, said "[I like] playing with other kids."

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Commissioner Greg Weiss urges parents to keep teens active after Wellington mall takeover threat
cards.teaser: A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting an increased law enforcement presence and responses from parents and a county commissioner.
cards.body:
A social media post promoting a teen takeover at Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to increase law enforcement presence at the mall on Friday. Shoppers noticed the heightened security, including Savanna Restrepo, who was picking up her son Isaac from summer camp. Restrepo said she had seen posts circulating online about the event beforehand and found the visible police presence reassuring. Fellow parent Eric Delgado also supported the law enforcement response. Teen takeovers are large gatherings of teens at malls, beaches or parks that typically devolve into violence, a trend spreading across Florida. An event in Clearwater at the end of May resulted in widespread property damage, fights and the shooting of a 17-year-old. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier called the events "unacceptable" and announced a plan to investigate and prosecute those responsible.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Greg Weiss said community safety is a priority but pointed to a root cause: kids need activities during school breaks. He urged parents to utilize the county's community rec centers that offer programming throughout the day at city and county facilities. Weiss acknowledged that summer camp costs can be a barrier for families and noted that Palm Beach County offers scholarship opportunities for summer camps. He emphasized parental involvement, telling parents to know what their kids are doing and maintain contact with them.

cards.headline: Transpire Help sees funding cuts slash clients in half as Pride on the Block fundraiser draws supporters in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: Pride on the Block filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit that provides substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals.
cards.body:
Transpire Help, a non-profit organization that provides substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals, held its largest fundraiser, Pride on the Block, at The Peach in West Palm Beach on Saturday. Founder Donna Weinberger said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated and safe. Weinberger emphasized that a significant portion of the community, especially gender diverse individuals, lack health insurance or funds to access traditional treatment. The fundraiser has become increasingly critical as cuts to government funding have reduced the number of people the organization can serve in half.

The event brought together neighbors, allies, and activists to support the LGBTQ+ community. Performer Liam Chambers, a drag king, credited Transpire Help with helping turn his life around, saying he is three years sober and would not have been able to perform without the organization's support. Community member Jack Cesivon said the organization's impact is undeniable, noting that Transpire Help has helped people who have no one else to turn to for assistance.

cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire reaches 125 acres, now 99% contained after weekend escalation
cards.teaser: A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown grew to 125 acres over the weekend before firefighters brought it under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service.
cards.body:
A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated significantly over the weekend before reaching near-total containment. Martin County Fire Rescue firefighters responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. on Friday, June 5. Crews quickly contained the initial blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened. The Florida Forest Service assisted by establishing plow lines to help stop the spread of flames, while MCFR's drone team identified remaining hotspots and confirmed full containment before crews cleared the area.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated when crews returned to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire in the same general area. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident, with shifting winds and dense vegetation contributing to rapid fire growth. A large-scale response from MCFR, FFS, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office ensued as firefighters worked to protect nearby structures. The fire reached approximately 125 acres in total size and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning. The Florida Forest Service remains on scene monitoring conditions. Officials noted early indications suggested it may have been a "holdover fire," where a lightning strike could have smoldered underground for days before igniting visible flames. The investigation into the fire's origin remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance overwhelmed with nearly 8,000 calls monthly as residents struggle with $2,020 average rent
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Community Services Department receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month, but has only $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department administers an Emergency Rental Assistance Program with nearly $2 million in combined grant funding to help residents unable to pay rent. Program director Dr. James Green told WPTV that the department receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance monthly and currently has about 800 applications in the queue. Applications open at the beginning of each month and typically fill within the first couple of hours, with the assistance portal frequently marked closed due to high demand. Green urged anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 monthly.

Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa after 12 years as an educator, switched to real estate hoping for higher income. She told WPTV she worries about paying rent almost every day as all bills rise except paychecks. Chellizabeth Colon, a 27-year-old pregnant mother, turned to WPTV for help after a split with her husband. She cannot work due to serious pregnancy complications. WPTV connected Colon with the Emergency Rental Assistance Program. Green said the recent surge in applications stems partly from rising costs of living including housing, gas, and food.

cards.headline: Florida voters to decide property tax rollback on November ballot after homestead exemption proposal draws mixed reactions
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, a proposal that needs 60% approval to pass.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners. The ballot measure would need 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018.

Reactions to the proposal have been mixed among West Palm Beach residents. Brian Edington supports the idea because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida and said he is comfortable with local governments spending less. He pointed to his own neighborhood as an example of where cuts could be made, noting that trash services pick up twice a week when once a week would be adequate. However, renters expressed skepticism about the proposal. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach renters, predicting that landlords will raise rent on all renters in response.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart for $50,000 after allegedly finding live worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections after finding live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee in June 2024.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard of Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter discovered live worms in SpaghettiOs they purchased in June 2024 from the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the complaint, both she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications following the incident. Hubbard documented the contamination in multiple videos that depict worm-like organisms actively moving within the food product, according to her attorneys.

The lawsuit against Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart seeks $50,000 in damages. The complaint alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks for 250th anniversary celebration due to severe drought conditions
cards.teaser: State leaders are watching drought conditions closely as they weigh whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence, with the entire state of Florida at least abnormally dry.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look significantly different this year as state leaders weigh whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence due to severe drought conditions. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was put in place. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with areas including Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing a range of moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about the possibility of a ban in May. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said. He acknowledged the significance of this year's holiday but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, the store has already seen increased customer activity ahead of the holiday. Bill Murphy of Sky King Fireworks said the store monitors drought conditions carefully but remains cautiously optimistic, noting there is plenty of rain in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island faces critical erosion threatening to split island at Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns Jupiter Island's entire 11.5-mile shoreline is critically eroded, with the ocean potentially breaking through at Peck Lake and splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely that ocean breakthrough at Peck Lake could split the island in half. The erosion threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach would transform a thin strip of land into an open inlet. This scenario has occurred before. In the early 1960s, a storm breached Peck Lake until the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. According to the report, the Joseph Reed Mound, an archaeological site between 3,000 and 4,000 years old, has already lost half its area to erosion. Wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park are also threatened. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society noted that over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas and that future breaches could destabilize ecosystems dependent on a careful balance between fresh and saltwater environments.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field acknowledged that sea level rise is factual, noting that rates have accelerated over the last 15 years. In April 2025, Jupiter Island completed a major beach renourishment project that deposited enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. The town spends approximately 3 million dollars in taxpayer money annually on beach renourishment. Field emphasized that current solutions are temporary fixes, stating "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over." He warned that if funding disappears, "the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly, and not in a way that anybody's particularly happy with."

Parents have responded positively to the club's arrival in the community. Thomas Furlong brought his children to participate because he saw it as an ideal opportunity for his daughter to learn chess while helping his son improve his existing skills. He also appreciated that the setting gave his children a chance to engage in friendly competition with each other. Francesca Furlong, one of the newest members, enjoys the social aspect most. "I like playing with other kids," she said about her favorite part of attending the club.

The Atlantis Chess Club is establishing itself as a fixture in the Port St. Lucie community through its weekly Friday meetings at the library. Looking ahead, the organization plans to expand its reach by launching two additional programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. This growth reflects the growing interest in chess among young people and suggests that Baptiste's initial vision of building respect for board games is resonating with families in the area.

cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire reaches 125 acres, now 99% contained after weekend escalation
cards.teaser: A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated significantly over the weekend, reaching 125 acres before firefighters brought it under near-total control by Sunday morning.
cards.body:
A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated significantly over the weekend before being brought under near-total control. Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. on Friday, June 5. Crews quickly contained the blaze at approximately 37.8 acres with no reported injuries and no structures threatened. The Florida Forest Service established plow lines to help stop the spread of flames, while MCFR's drone team identified remaining hotspots.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated when crews returned to the same general area to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident. Shifting winds and dense vegetation contributed to rapid fire growth, prompting a large-scale response from MCFR, FFS and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Firefighters worked to protect nearby structures as smoke spread across the area. The fire reached approximately 125 acres in total size and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning. Early indications suggest the fire may have been a holdover fire, meaning a lightning strike could have smoldered underground for days before igniting visible flames. The Florida Forest Service remains in the area monitoring conditions and continues investigating the fire's origin.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach hosts Pride on the Block to support LGBTQ+ community and fund crucial services
cards.teaser: Pride on the Block filled The Peach in West Palm Beach on Saturday, serving as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit providing treatment, mental health care and housing to LGBTQ+ individuals.
cards.body:
Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists at The Peach in West Palm Beach on Saturday to support the LGBTQ+ community and raise funds for Transpire Help, a non-profit organization that provides substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated, filled with unity, joy, and happiness in one spot where they feel safe. Cortney Salley, an LGBTQ+ community member, said it was a great feeling to be around people in the community and express how you want to be represented.

For performer Liam Chambers, the event held deep personal meaning. Chambers credits Transpire Help with turning his life around, noting he is three years sober and now performs as a drag king, which he would not have been able to do without the organization. Weinberger explained that the services are especially critical for those without access to traditional health care resources, as a big part of the community, especially gender diverse people, do not have health insurance or funds to access treatment. The fundraiser is more important than ever because cuts to government funding have slashed the number of people the organization can help in half. Jack Cesivon said Transpire Help has helped people who literally have nobody, while Jake Jayalin Eggert said being there allows him to be amongst people who hear and see him in one of the most authentic experiences.

hero.headline: Beetlejuice Musical Playing at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach Through June 7
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit Beetlejuice the musical is running at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach through June 7, with actor Ryan Stajmiger playing the mischievous demon from Tim Burton's 1988 film.
hero.body:
From wigs gone rogue to audience laughter echoing through the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, Beetlejuice the musical has landed at the Kravis Center. Running June 2 through June 7, the Broadway hit brings its spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments to Palm Beach County. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen, whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. Very early in the run, he experienced one of those unexpected moments. He has a wig change on stage and is wearing two wigs. The second wig came off with the first wig, so he was bald for an entire scene, and got to play with that a little bit, and got to experience everyone seeing him for the first time and not knowing that he is bald.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50, and the safest and most secure way to get them is to buy directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: 100 Paddlers to Cross 80 Miles of Atlantic Ocean from Bahamas to Lake Worth Beach for Cystic Fibrosis
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the Atlantic Ocean this June in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. The group will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13 and arrive at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. Event founder Travis Suit created the endurance trek to benefit the Piper's Angels Foundation, which he established in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The four-day event begins June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner. Friday features a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis patients, followed by rest and safety checks before the midnight launch. All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, with mandatory safety meetings held before departure. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000, while crew and virtual participants have a $500 minimum, with contributions due by July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong beach celebration. For more information, visit crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

hero.headline: Florida Home Builders Association endorses Ashley Moody for U.S. Senate
hero.body:
The Florida Home Builders Association announced its endorsement of U.S. Senator Ashley Moody on Monday as she runs in the November general election. Moody, a Plant City Republican, was appointed to the Senate by Governor Ron DeSantis to fill the seat left vacant when Marco Rubio was confirmed as Secretary of State. This year's election will determine who serves the final two years of the six-year Senate term.

In response to the endorsement, Moody expressed her appreciation for the organization's support. "I am honored to earn the endorsement of the Florida Home Builders Association – an organization that represents the men and women who quite literally build the American Dream for Florida families," she said. Moody highlighted her work on housing issues, stating she has championed housing reform and fought to lower costs for Florida families. The construction industry has backed Moody before, endorsing her during her 2018 and 2022 campaigns for Florida Attorney General, races in which she received more votes than any candidate on the Florida ballot.

Moody has already raised substantial campaign funds for her Senate bid. Through March of this year, she had accumulated 8.2 million dollars. In the Republican primary, she faces three other candidates, though her closest competitor had raised less than 3,400 dollars by the end of March. The GOP primary will take place in August to determine the party's nominee.

On the Democratic side, Alex Vindman is positioned as the likely nominee after raising approximately 8.2 million dollars through the first quarter. However, Vindman must first compete in the Democratic primary against Angie Nixon, who had reported 294,000 dollars in fundraising through the same period. The August primary elections will decide which candidates from each party advance to the November general election, where voters will select Florida's representative for the remainder of the Senate term. Moody is seeking her first full six-year Senate term following her two successful statewide campaigns for Attorney General.

cards.headline: Florida childhood poverty drops by 200,000 since Prosperity Initiative launch
cards.teaser: Florida has reduced the number of children living in poverty by more than 200,000 since launching the Florida Prosperity Initiative, though 16.5% of the state's children still live in poverty.
cards.body:
More than 200,000 fewer Florida children are living in poverty since the launch of the Florida Prosperity Initiative, according to the State of Childhood Poverty in Florida report. However, 16.5% of Florida children still live in poverty, with 711,576 children affected statewide. Over half of these children are concentrated in just 152 of Florida's 983 ZIP codes, representing 15% of the state's total ZIP codes. Hillsborough County demonstrated the largest single-year reduction in childhood poverty in Florida, with 3,971 fewer children living in poverty in 2024 than in 2023. In the Tampa Bay region, disparities remain stark. In Hillsborough County's 33612 ZIP code, 3,912 children live in poverty, the highest concentration in the area, while only 37 children live in poverty in ZIP code 33606.

The Florida Prosperity Initiative focuses on 10 Root Causes of Poverty, including access to meals, behavioral and mental health services, stable housing, and workforce training. Mark Wilson, President and CEO of the Florida Chamber of Commerce and Foundation, said Florida aims to become the 10th-largest global economy by 2030 and cut childhood poverty in half, as outlined in the Florida 2030 Blueprint. The Florida Chamber Foundation is hosting the 2026 Florida Prosperity Economic Opportunity Solution Summit on June 9 in Tampa to examine actionable, data-driven strategies that expand economic opportunities at the ZIP code level.

cards.headline: Five competitive Florida House seats remain unchallenged days before qualifying deadline
cards.teaser: With the qualifying deadline less than a week away, five competitive Florida House districts have candidates from only one major party running, including districts decided by margins of 11 percentage points or less in 2024.
cards.body:
Less than a week before the June 13 qualifying deadline, 25 Florida House district races remain uncontested by one of the two major political parties. While 80 percent of these races occur in heavily partisan districts where challenging would waste resources, five competitive House districts have attracted candidates from only one major party. Two are Republican-controlled and three are Democrat-led, with narrow voter divides that make the lack of opposition notable. They range from a Palm Beach County district that sided with Kamala Harris by just 1 percentage point, based on analyses by Matt Isbell of MCI Maps, to an Orange County district Harris won by 11 points. The margin in the Orange County race mirrors the 10-point advantage Donald Trump held in House District 87, which Democratic Rep. Emily Gregory flipped in a March upset. The other three uncontested competitive races are located in Duval, Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties.

The Florida Democratic Party stated it has worked to identify strong candidates and invested in year-round organizing, with over 1,300 Democrats expressing interest in running over the last 18 months. Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power said his party remains focused on winning races and expressed confidence in growing the GOP's legislative supermajority. Power stated the Florida Democrats are on the verge of extinction and that Republicans will field quality candidates across Florida. The Primary Election is scheduled for August 18, followed by the General Election.

cards.headline: Navy reserve officer Dan Green enters Congressional District 9 race with $1 million
cards.teaser: Dan Green, a Navy reserve officer and former Pentagon appointee, launched a campaign for Florida's 9th Congressional District with $1 million in self-funding.
cards.body:
Dan Green, a Navy reserve officer and Pentagon appointee under President Donald Trump, announced a campaign for Florida's 9th Congressional District as the state's congressional qualifying week opened. The Vero Beach Republican said he is putting $1 million of his own money into the race and has the backing of the War Veterans Fund, the group he co-founded in 2018 to elect veterans to Congress. Green spent 23 years in the Navy, mobilized for tours in Afghanistan and Iraq, and was appointed Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Strategy and Force Development in 2019, a role on the team that writes the National Defense Strategy.

The redrawn CD 9 has become a major GOP target after redistricting changed the district's politics dramatically. Under the old lines it was an Osceola-anchored, Hispanic-majority district that Democrat Darren Soto held comfortably since 2017. Ron DeSantis' new map stretched it south through the middle of the peninsula and east to absorb all of Indian River County, Green's home turf. Florida Politics analysis found Trump would have won the redrawn seat with more than 58%. Soto is running again as the only incumbent in the contest. Green joins a Republican primary that includes retired Marine and former F-18 pilot Justin Story, who has qualified by petition, and 2024 nominee Thomas Chalifoux.

cards.headline: Florida congressional candidates qualify for 2026 ballot through petition route
cards.teaser: Multiple Florida congressional candidates have qualified for the 2026 ballot by collecting the required 2,564 verified voter petitions, demonstrating grassroots support ahead of qualifying deadline.
cards.body:
Congressional candidates in Florida have two paths to the 2026 ballot: filing fees or petition signatures. The petition route requires 2,564 verified signatures from registered voters in a district, collected by hand and submitted to Supervisors of Elections for verification against voter rolls. Campaigns typically lose 20% or more of gathered signatures during the disqualification process. The method requires volunteers, paid circulators, or both, and demonstrates a campaign's infrastructure and grassroots reach before voters cast ballots.

Several candidates have already qualified through petitions. Democrat Ronnie Murchinson-Rivera qualified for Congressional District 6, billed as the first congressional candidate in Florida to do so this cycle. A career first responder and former law enforcement officer, he is seeking his party's nomination to challenge Randy Fine in the reliably Republican district spanning Flagler and Volusia counties. Retired Marine Corps officer Justin Story announced 2,577 verified petitions for Congressional District 9, joining at least seven Republicans seeking to challenge Democratic incumbent Darren Soto. Maxwell Frost cleared the petition threshold for his third term in Congressional District 10, collecting signatures from voters across 30 Florida counties. Fort Lauderdale Democrat Oliver Larkin qualified with 3,042 verified signatures for Congressional District 24 to challenge incumbent Jared Moskowitz, while George Moraitis, a Fort Lauderdale attorney and former state Representative, qualified for Congressional District 25 as a Republican.

cards.headline: Florida sees one in five children still living in poverty despite recent progress
cards.teaser: Florida's childhood poverty rate stands at 16.5%, with disparities concentrated in specific ZIP codes across the state, according to a new analysis from the Florida Prosperity Initiative.
cards.body:
Florida still has one in five children living in poverty, with 16.5% of the state's 711,576 children affected, according to the Florida Prosperity Initiative's State of Childhood Poverty in Florida report. More than half of these children are concentrated in just 152 of Florida's 983 ZIP codes, with dramatic disparities visible in the Tampa Bay region. In Hillsborough County's 33612 ZIP code, 3,912 children live in poverty, the highest concentration in the area, while nearby ZIP code 33606 has only 37 children in poverty. Despite these challenges, Hillsborough County demonstrated that progress is possible, recording the largest reduction in childhood poverty in Florida over the past year, with 3,971 fewer children living in poverty in 2024 than in 2023.

The report identifies 10 Root Causes of Poverty affecting Florida families, including access to meals, stable housing, behavioral and mental health services, and healthcare. These issues are interconnected: children struggling with hunger are more likely to face academic challenges, families without stable housing often experience employment and education disruptions, and limited healthcare access creates long-term financial instability. Mark Wilson, President and CEO of the Florida Chamber of Commerce and Foundation, emphasized that reducing childhood poverty is essential to Florida's goal of becoming the 10th-largest global economy by 2030 and strengthening the state's future workforce.

cards.headline: Florida campaigns enter final week of qualifying period for 2026 elections
cards.teaser: Florida candidates have until June 13 to qualify for federal, state, and local offices in the 2026 election cycle.
cards.body:
Florida's qualifying period for the 2026 election cycle concludes in four days, with the deadline set for June 13. Candidates seeking positions in federal, gubernatorial, cabinet, state, and local offices must officially enter their races by that date to appear on the August 18 primary ballot and the November general election ballot.

Twenty-five Florida House district races currently lack major party opposition, with one party running unopposed in each contest. While most of these uncontested seats are in heavily partisan districts where one party holds a significant advantage, five competitive House districts present a notable gap. These districts in Palm Beach, Orange, Duval, Miami-Dade, and Pinellas counties had narrow voter divides in 2024, with presidential margins ranging from 1 to 11 percentage points. The Palm Beach County district sided with Kamala Harris by just 1 point, while the Orange County district favored Harris by 11 points, roughly the same margin by which Donald Trump won House District 87. Of four uncontested Senate races, only Senate District 36 in Miami-Dade County is considered competitive, where Ileana Garcia won her seat in 2020 by 34 votes.

hero.headline: Stuart business owner says city permit delays cost her $40,000 over two years
hero.body:
A Stuart business owner is speaking out about what she describes as an unnecessarily complicated permit approval process for a storage building project. Janet Milici, who co-owns Natural Flow Impact Windows and Doors, decided to share her experience after attending a community meeting in Jensen Beach. She filed her initial application in 2024 to construct a 30-by-40-foot storage building at the back of her business property. The structure was designed to store materials used in her day-to-day operations, not to expand the business itself.

Throughout the permitting process, Milici faced multiple requirements that she believes went beyond what was necessary for a simple storage building. The city required her to complete engineering studies, environmental reviews, and traffic analyses. She was also required to pay for turtle relocation. All of these additional steps added up financially, with Milici estimating she has spent approximately $40,000 to navigate the approval process. While she understands that permitting requirements exist for good reasons, Milici believes the demands placed on her project have been excessive. "All I am trying to do is improve my property. I am trying to improve the service we can give our customers, and it's like the city is shooting us down at every turn," she said.

The timing of the delays has created a significant problem for her business operations. With hurricane season now underway, materials that should be stored safely inside the building remain exposed outdoors. This vulnerability concerns Milici, who worries about potential damage and the financial impact on her company. "The thing that bothers me is that hurricane season is here, and if I can't put my materials in a safe place, then it's going to cost me—it's going to put me out of business if you really want to know," she said. Despite her frustrations with the process, Milici emphasized that she chose to pursue proper permitting rather than cut corners. "People try to cut corners and do things without permitting, but we are trying to do everything right," she noted.

The permit has recently received approval, but Milici still faces additional city fees as the project enters its final stages. She felt her situation was important enough to bring to public attention, hoping others in the area would become aware of the challenges involved in the local permitting process. WPTV reached out to the City of Stuart's Planning and Zoning department for comment on the permit procedures for storage buildings within city limits but has not yet received a response.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County approves Project Orchid manufacturing complex
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County has approved a large manufacturing complex known as Project Orchid.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners have approved Project Orchid, a major manufacturing complex development coming to the area. The approval represents a significant industrial expansion for St. Lucie County and marks an important milestone in the project's advancement toward construction and operation.

The commissioners' decision to greenlight Project Orchid reflects the county's commitment to attracting substantial manufacturing operations and economic development. The project has moved forward through the approval process, clearing a key regulatory hurdle that will allow the development to proceed. This authorization from county leadership demonstrates support for the industrial initiative among local government officials.

The approval of Project Orchid is expected to contribute to the region's economic growth and industrial base. Large manufacturing complexes such as this typically bring job creation, increased tax revenue, and expanded commercial activity to the areas where they operate. St. Lucie County's authorization of the project positions the region to benefit from these potential economic advantages.

The commissioners' action on Project Orchid adds to recent development activity in St. Lucie County. The region has seen various infrastructure and community improvements in recent months, reflecting ongoing growth and investment in the area. With this manufacturing complex now approved, St. Lucie County continues its trajectory as a destination for significant business and industrial projects that contribute to the local economy and community development.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old launches junior chess club at St. Lucie West Library
cards.teaser: A new juniors chess club has launched in Port St.
cards.body:
A new juniors chess club has launched in Port St. Lucie, inspired by 9-year-old Orion Jean Baptiste, who wanted to share his love of the game with his community. Baptiste's passion for chess began at age 5 playing alongside family. "I just wanted kids to learn about chess," Baptiste said. He hopes to pass that passion on to others, noting that many people are focused on technology instead. "I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games," he said.

The Atlantis Chess Club now meets every Friday at the St. Lucie West Library and has attracted more than 36 juniors of all skill levels. Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, said chess will help develop the next generation by building "leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision making." Thomas Furlong brought his children to the club, calling it "the perfect chance for her to learn chess, my son to get better at chess and then them to have a little sibling rivalry competition." For new member Francesca Furlong, the best part is "playing with other kids." The club will soon begin two more programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County approves $2.7 million public dock on St. Lucie River
cards.teaser: A $2.7 million public dock project on the St. Lucie River has received county approval.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County has approved a $2.7 million public dock to be built on the St. Lucie River. The project will provide public access to the river for county residents and visitors.

The dock represents a significant investment in waterfront access for the county. Details about the specific location along the St.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce parking enforcement targets downtown visitors staying more than 2 hours
cards.teaser: Downtown Fort Pierce guests who park for more than two hours are receiving hefty citations from city enforcement.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce has begun issuing citations to downtown visitors who park for more than two hours. The enforcement targets guests in the downtown area who exceed the time limit.

The citations carry substantial fines for violators. The parking enforcement reflects Fort Pierce's efforts to manage downtown parking availability for businesses and visitors.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested for allegedly chasing children with baseball bat
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man faces arrest after allegedly chasing children with a baseball bat.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested a man accused of chasing children while armed with a baseball bat. The incident prompted law enforcement response and led to the man's arrest.

Details about the circumstances of the incident, the number of children involved, and specific charges filed against the suspect were not provided in available records. The arrest took place in Port St. Lucie.

cards.headline: Two Port St. Lucie Girl Scouts earn highest honor
cards.teaser: Two Girl Scouts from Port St. Lucie have achieved the prestigious highest honor in the organization.
cards.body:
Two Girl Scouts from Port St. Lucie have earned the highest honor available in Girl Scouts. The achievement represents years of dedication and service work by both scouts.

The highest honor in Girl Scouts recognizes exceptional leadership and community service. The two Port St. Lucie scouts join a select group of young women who have achieved this distinction.

cards.headline: North Causeway Bridge in Fort Pierce set to open May 15
cards.teaser: The new North Causeway Bridge in Fort Pierce will open to traffic on May 15.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce's new North Causeway Bridge is scheduled to open May 15. The bridge represents a major infrastructure project for the city and will provide updated access across the waterway.

The new bridge replaces the existing North Causeway crossing. Details about construction costs and specific improvements to the new span were not available in records.

hero.headline: Indian River County voters face decision on renewing $40 lagoon tax
hero.body:
Indian River County residents will decide whether to renew a $40 annual tax dedicated to Indian River Lagoon restoration efforts. The tax generates funding for lagoon cleanup and environmental restoration projects that have been underway in the county.

The renewal vote will determine whether gains made in lagoon restoration continue or face potential setbacks. The tax assessment has funded local environmental initiatives aimed at improving water quality and habitat restoration in the Indian River Lagoon system.

The Indian River Lagoon spans multiple counties along Florida's east coast and has faced ongoing environmental challenges requiring sustained restoration funding. Indian River County's portion of the restoration work depends on the continuation of the local tax revenue stream.

Voters will make their decision on the $40 annual assessment renewal in an upcoming ballot measure. The tax has been a dedicated revenue source for lagoon restoration work in Indian River County since its initial approval.

cards.headline: Sebastian Pines zoning proposal advances to City Council
cards.teaser: A zoning matter involving Sebastian Pines is moving forward to the Sebastian City Council for consideration.
cards.body:
The Sebastian City Council will take up a zoning issue related to Sebastian Pines. The proposal has advanced through the review process and is now headed to the council for action.

The zoning matter involves the Sebastian Pines development. City Council members will consider the proposal at an upcoming meeting.

Sebastian officials will review the zoning request as part of the regular council agenda. The item has completed preliminary review and is ready for council consideration.

cards.headline: Indian River Firefighters Fair donates $2,500 to local burn victim
cards.teaser: The Indian River Burn Fund provided $2,500 from Firefighters Fair proceeds to help a local burn victim.
cards.body:
The Firefighters Fair donated $2,500 from the Indian River Burn Fund to a local burn victim. The contribution comes from funds raised through the annual Firefighters Fair event in Indian River County.

The Indian River Burn Fund supports local residents who have suffered burn injuries. The fund provides financial assistance to help victims and their families during recovery.

The $2,500 donation represents proceeds collected during the Firefighters Fair. The event serves as a fundraiser for the burn fund, which directly benefits Indian River County residents in need of assistance.
